extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral/political philosophy (those studying Aristotle's Ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging human conduct and the formation of moral character according to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (as explained in the introduction and notes). Focuses on what constitutes the good life, how virtues are formed, and what counts as right action and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as the supreme end (eudaimonia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of all action is the greatest happiness of the greatest number; the good towards which all human desires and practical activities are directed is 'Happiness' (Welfare or Well‑being).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness is the practical/achievable good conformable to man's nature and circumstances; it is the aim of practical knowledge and political organisation. It is not identical with mere physical pleasure, honour, wealth, or Platonic other‑worldly goods. External conditions (length of life, wealth, luck) affect attainability but are secondary to the development and exercise of relevant powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness consists in activity of function in accordance with reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Human happiness lies in activity or energising in a way peculiar to man — the activity of a being who possesses reason and applies it; it presupposes development (not merely possession) of relevant powers and capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chief determinant of success in life is acquiring and exercising certain powers (virtues). Happiness is practical rather than merely theoretical; the exercise of intellectual and moral excellences constitutes the good life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between intellectual and moral virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues split into Goodnesses of Intellect (excellences of reason) and Goodnesses of Character (moral virtues regulating impulses and feelings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual virtues are acquired by study and instruction; moral virtues are acquired by habituation and discipline. Both excite admiration and are acquired qualities rather than innate endowments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtue defined as a stable state obeying a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral virtue is a permanent state of the agent (a steady self‑imposed obedience to a rule of action accepted by the agent for recurrent situations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue is not mere feeling or natural aptitude; it requires knowledge of the rule, acceptance of it as the agent's own, and repeated action conforming to it until it becomes 'second nature.' The exact amount appropriate in each case is set by reason and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habituation as the means of character formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Character (good or bad) is produced by habituation — the repeated doing of acts with similar quality which, acting on natural propensities, fix them toward good or evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character formation needs discipline, external guidance, imitation, and practice rather than mere intellectual instruction or leaving it to nature. Right acts must be performed in the right way and repeated to form virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of the Mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Rightness in feeling or action is adaptation/adjustment to the special requirements of a situation — quantitatively, doing or feeling 'just the amount required' (neither excess nor defect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each virtue is a mean between two vices (excess and deficiency). Rules can indicate the mean as a principle of arrangement, but the precise amount for an individual situation must be determined by practical intuition; the doctrine is a classificatory device more than a precise formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical wisdom (phronesis) as the intellectual virtue of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical wisdom apprehends the right rules of conduct and supplies the rationale linking means to the end (happiness); it is the intellectual excellency that produces and justifies right practical rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical wisdom is interdependent with moral virtue: it presupposes a formed character and in turn helps produce right action. True practical wisdom is not mere cleverness and includes the capacity to generate the right rule promptly and to justify it by showing its relation to the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of conduct are general and probabilistic, not exact
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical or moral rules state probabilities and admit exceptions; the subject‑matter of conduct lacks mathematical exactness and uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect absolute uniformities or rigid derivations; moral rules guide action but require experience and situational judgment. Overreliance on abstract universal reasoning without experience is a mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience/practice as necessary source and test
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience (moral experience: possession and exercise of good character) is necessary truly to understand moral principles and to apply them profitably; practice validates principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical apprehension alone is insufficient; rules are tested and formed through repeated application in real life. The faculty that attains truth in practical matters (nous) is grounded in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness and responsibility (voluntary vs involuntary acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coercion and ignorance of relevant circumstances render acts involuntary and exempt the doer from responsibility; otherwise acts are voluntary and the agent is responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither passion nor ignorance of the right rule necessarily extenuates responsibility. Distinguish between voluntary acts and those done from set choice (deliberation). Inner consent and choice are central to moral responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation and choice as markers of deliberate action
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation involves thinking about means to ends; acts done of set choice involve deliberation and reflect the agent's whole nature — they are the most significant evidence of what he is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate acts presuppose inner consent and are closely tied to responsibility. Distinguish between mere impulse and actions grounded in deliberative choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as a civic moral virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice (in Aristotle's restricted sense) is a special goodness of character required of every adult citizen for the administration and judicial functions of the civic community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This treatment focuses on justice as temper/attitude for civic participation (juryman/administrator), not on the broader metaphysical or large political distribution of power. Distinguish distributive justice (division of gains among claimants) from corrective justice (legal redress); mathematical precision attempts may confuse the treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as a complement to morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship (philia) is a necessary and attractive complement to the account of morality and has its own types and metaphysical aspects relevant to practical life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship provides mutual society, help, and comfort in prosperity and adversity; its treatment illuminates social aspects of moral life and enriches the understanding of character and flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure's proper role (not identical with happiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is not to be identified with Happiness; while pleasures are good under certain amounts and conditions, excessive or misapplied pleasure is not the supreme good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject hedonistic identifications of happiness; pleasures can contribute but must be subordinated to the rationally determined good. Beware both those who overemphasise pleasure's badness and those who exaggerate its value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incontinence (akrasia) and weakness of will
rubrics_metrics.description: Incontinence is the condition where an agent knows what is good but chronically fails to act on that knowledge; desire may have rational elements that mislead the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle analyses causes (e.g., passions suggesting false minor premises) but does not fully solve the paradox. Recognise that lack of self‑control involves competing reasons and that the will may be divided even when knowledge is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral rules permit variety and require situational intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Although rules prescribe rightness, they do not prescribe mechanical uniformity; each rule allows for variety within limits and requires the agent's intuition to determine the exact measure in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trying to reduce moral decision‑making to a single monotonous type or formula; practical judgment at the particular moment is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtues concern recurring, grouped situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations fall into groups constituting the 'fields' of the several moral virtues; for each there is a rule conformity to which secures rightness in individual acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the relevant class of recurrent situations for a virtue and apply the accepted rule, while adjusting to particulars by intuition and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of character and practical wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: True practical wisdom and true goodness of character are interdependent; neither is completely present without the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical wisdom presupposes moral virtue (so perception of ends and conditions requires formed character), while moral virtue requires the guidance of practical wisdom to produce consistent right action.

rubrics_metrics.name: The moral ideal as the object of desire rather than duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral ideal is identified with the object of desire (happiness) — what we actually desire and which would satisfy human desire — rather than presented primarily as duty imposed by a superior power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shifts emphasis from duty‑centric ethics to a teleological, desire‑aligned conception of the good; moral education must cultivate proper desires and appetites as well as rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: External conditions influence but do not determine happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of life, wealth and good luck are conditions that affect the attainability of happiness but do not constitute it; the primary determinant is what the person makes of his nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating someone's prospects for eudaimonia, account for both internal character development and external circumstantial constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing types of justice or overmathematizing moral concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to give precise mathematical forms to principles (especially in justice) can confuse rather than clarify; many of Aristotle's distinctions (distributive vs corrective) are practical, not metaphysical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distinctions as pragmatic analytic tools for ordinary civic problems rather than as rigid formal formulas; be cautious about forcing precise numerical analogies onto moral judgments.
